chief_complaint: severe dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and chronic pelvic pain
hpi_details: A 29-year-old female presents to the clinic with severe dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and chronic pelvic pain. The symptoms have developed over time and are gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks she may have chronic internal scarring or pelvic inflammation left behind by a severe bladder infection she had years ago.
concerns: She is worried that the pain during intercourse will strain her marriage and prevent her from ever getting pregnant.
expectations: She hopes to get stronger prescription pain medication and a referral to a specialist who can investigate why her cramps are so severe.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Pelvic endometriosis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Endometriosis pelvic: Oral contraceptives, NSAIDs, diagnostic laparoscopy if severe, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: severe dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and chronic pelvic pain

Key HPI features: A 29-year-old female presents to the clinic with severe dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and chronic pelvic pain. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Endometriosis pelvic.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Pelvic endometriosis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Adenomyosis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Chronic pain unresponsive to NSAIDs.
management_principles: Use NSAIDs and, when pregnancy is not currently desired and there are no contraindications, consider hormonal suppression; consider laparoscopy when it will guide management
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: Patient with severe dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and chronic pelvic pain consistent with endometriosis.

must_ask.objective: Characterize the chronic pelvic pain pattern
must_ask.say: Is the pain constant, or does it worsen specifically around your period?
Do you have pain during or after intercourse?
What medications have you already tried for the pain?
How is this pain affecting your work and daily activities?
If medication doesn't control your symptoms, a diagnostic laparoscopy can confirm and treat endometriosis.

history.answer: I have been dealing with terrible menstrual cramps, constant aching in my lower belly, and severe pain during sex that just keeps getting worse.
I had ordinary cramps as a teenager, but this severe and debilitating pain began about two years ago and has been escalating steadily.
The cramps start two or three days before bleeding, last the entire period, and lately a dull ache lingers even between my periods.
history.topic: Timing of pain relative to menses

history.answer: It feels like a deep, throbbing, twisting ache in my lower pelvis that radiates into my lower back and down the front of my thighs.
During my period it reaches an 8 or 9 out of 10. I often have to take time off work and stay in bed with a heating pad.
Yes, it has become noticeably worse month after month over the past year.
I take ibuprofen 400 milligrams up to three times a day, but it barely takes the edge off anymore. I have not tried birth control pills.
I feel nauseous and very bloated during the worst days, but I haven't vomited. I also feel drained and tired all the time.
My bleeding volume is normal and I do not pass large blood clots, nor do I have bleeding between periods.
Yes, having sex causes deep, sharp pain inside my pelvis. It hurts so much that I have been avoiding intimacy lately.
Having a bowel movement during my period is quite painful and crampy, but urinating feels normal without any burning.
history.topic: Pain with urination or bowel movements

history.answer: The pain during sex is putting so much strain on my relationship, and I am scared it means I will never be able to have a baby.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, or unusual vaginal discharge.
No, I haven't had any sudden stabbing pain on one side, lightheadedness, or fainting episodes.
My first period was when I was 13. My cycles come regularly every 28 to 30 days and bleeding lasts about 5 days.
I have been in a committed relationship with one partner for three years, and neither of us has ever had a sexually transmitted infection.
We use condoms for contraception. I have never used an intrauterine device or contraceptive implants.
My mother suffered from severe menstrual cramps for years and had surgery for endometriosis in her thirties.
Even when I am not bleeding, there is a persistent, dull ache across my lower pelvis that never completely goes away.
I feel exhausted and sluggish almost every day, probably because the ongoing pain disrupts my sleep and daily activities.
I have always been healthy and have no chronic medical conditions like high blood pressure or diabetes.
I have never had surgery, and I have never been hospitalized.
I do not take any regular prescription medications, just over-the-counter painkillers when the cramps get unbearable.
I do not have any allergies to medications, foods, or other substances.
I have never smoked cigarettes. I only drink an occasional glass of wine on social occasions.
I work as an office administrator and I live in an apartment with my partner.
My last period started exactly two weeks ago, and there is no chance that I could be pregnant right now.
history.topic: Last menstrual period and pregnancy possibility

history.answer: I keep thinking maybe that horrible urinary tract infection I had a couple of years ago caused lasting inflammation or scar tissue inside.
The pain during sex is putting so much strain on my relationship, and I am scared it means I will never be able to have a baby.
I am hoping you can refer me to a gynecologist and prescribe something stronger than regular over-the-counter painkillers so I can function.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, heart rate 74 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert, oriented, mildly fatigued and uncomfortable, but in no acute distress.
Conjunctivae are pink without pallor; sclerae are white and anicteric.
Abdomen is flat and symmetrical with no scars, distension, or visible pulsations.
Normoactive bowel sounds heard in all four quadrants; no abdominal bruits.
Soft with moderate deep tenderness in the suprapubic area and bilateral lower quadrants, without involuntary guarding or rigidity.
No rebound tenderness elicited in any abdominal quadrant.
No tenderness to percussion over either costovertebral angle.
Tenderness and palpable nodularity along the uterosacral ligaments and posterior fornix, fixed retroverted uterus, and mild bilateral adnexal tenderness without cervical motion tenderness.
